lesson.title: Two Kinds of Smart That Age Differently
lesson.summary: Fluid intelligence is the raw ability to reason and solve novel problems, while crystallized intelligence is accumulated knowledge and skill, and the two follow different trajectories across the lifespan.
lesson.body:
Not all forms of intelligence behave the same way as people age, and one of the most useful distinctions for understanding this comes from psychologist Raymond Cattell, later developed further with John Horn. Fluid intelligence is the capacity to reason abstractly, solve novel problems, spot patterns, and think flexibly in situations you have not encountered before, largely independent of what you have already learned. Crystallized intelligence is the opposite side of the coin: the accumulated knowledge, vocabulary, facts, and skills a person has built up over a lifetime of learning and experience. This builds directly on the broader concept of general intelligence, or the g factor, which describes a single underlying factor that tends to make people who score well on one type of cognitive task also score relatively well on others. Fluid and crystallized intelligence can be thought of as two major, related components that contribute to that general ability, distinguished by where the ability comes from and how it holds up over time.

A useful shorthand is that fluid intelligence is about processing new information quickly and flexibly, while crystallized intelligence is about applying what you already know. A timed test with novel puzzles, matrices, or unfamiliar logic problems mostly taps fluid intelligence. A vocabulary test, or a test asking you to recall historical facts or apply a well-practiced skill, mostly taps crystallized intelligence. Most real-world thinking, of course, draws on both at once.

This distinction matters enormously for understanding adult and aging development, because fluid and crystallized intelligence do not age the same way. Fluid intelligence tends to peak relatively early in adulthood and then shows a gradual decline with age, a pattern researchers generally attribute to changes in processing speed and other basic cognitive mechanics that come with brain aging. Crystallized intelligence, by contrast, tends to hold steady or even continue increasing well into later adulthood, since it reflects a lifetime of accumulated knowledge that does not depend on quick novel processing. This is one reason older adults often remain excellent at tasks that draw on deep expertise and accumulated vocabulary, even as they may become slower at rapid novel problem-solving. The pattern is not universal or perfectly linear for every individual, and factors like health, education, and continued mental engagement all play a role, but the general fluid-declines, crystallized-holds-steady trend is one of the more consistently replicated findings in the psychology of aging and intelligence.
